explanation.whyCorrect: The very high-attenuation (bright white) foci on CT are calcium deposits. Coronary and aortic valve calcification commonly accompany degenerative aortic stenosis and are quantified as a calcium score.

questions.stem: This transverse gross section of the heart from a patient with long-standing aortic stenosis shows a characteristic ventricular remodeling pattern. What is it?

choices.text: Amyloid infiltration causing a stiff non-hypertrophied wall

choices.label: B
choices.text: Eccentric hypertrophy with a dilated thin-walled chamber

choices.label: D
choices.text: Right ventricular hypertrophy from pulmonary hypertension

choices.label: E
choices.text: Acute transmural myocardial infarction with wall thinning

explanation.summary: Chronic pressure overload from a stenotic aortic valve drives parallel sarcomere addition, producing concentric LV hypertrophy: a markedly thickened wall without chamber dilation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chronic pressure overload from a stenotic aortic valve drives parallel sarcomere addition, producing concentric LV hypertrophy: a markedly thickened wall without chamber dilation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Amyloid also thickens the wall but is an infiltrative process; aortic stenosis causes true myocyte hypertrophy from pressure overload.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Eccentric hypertrophy with a dilated chamber results from volume overload, such as regurgitant valve disease, not stenosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Right ventricular hypertrophy follows pulmonary hypertension, whereas aortic stenosis loads the left ventricle.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Acute infarction causes regional necrosis and thinning, not uniform wall thickening.

explanation.whyCorrect: The cusps are heaped up with rigid calcific nodules that restrict opening, reducing the effective orifice area. This degenerative calcific process is the leading cause of aortic stenosis in older adults.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Vegetations are friable masses attached to cusps, rather than rigid, heaped-up calcific nodules restricting opening.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Myxomatous mitral prolapse shows floppy, redundant mitral leaflets, not rigid nodular semilunar cusps.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Rheumatic mitral stenosis produces a fish-mouth mitral orifice with commissural fusion and chordal thickening, not nodular semilunar cusps.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A normal tricuspid aortic valve has thin, pliable cusps and a wide orifice, not thickened rigid nodules.

choices.text: Progressive fibrocalcific thickening of the cusps

choices.text: Fatty streak deposition within the lumen only

choices.label: E

whyWrongByChoice.B: Fatty streaks are early atherosclerotic lesions of the arterial intima, not the process that thickens valve cusps.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Infective vegetations cause valve destruction and regurgitation rather than gradual fibrocalcific narrowing over decades.

choices.label: A
choices.text: End-diastolic volume falls while stroke volume is preserved

choices.label: B
choices.text: Stroke volume is unchanged because preload compensates fully

choices.label: C
choices.text: Isovolumetric relaxation is eliminated, raising output

choices.label: D
choices.text: Stroke volume rises as the aorta accepts more blood

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stroke volume falls because the ventricle must generate higher pressure to eject

explanation.whyCorrect: A pressure-overload state raises the pressure at which the aortic valve opens, so ejection occurs against a higher load. For a given contractility the loop narrows and stroke volume decreases.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Increased afterload raises end-systolic volume rather than reducing end-diastolic volume while stroke volume stays preserved.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Acute afterload increase reduces ejection; preload compensation is incomplete, so stroke volume falls.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Isovolumetric relaxation still occurs with increased afterload, and the loop narrows rather than output rising.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Higher afterload means the ventricle ejects against more resistance, so less blood is ejected.

whyWrongByChoice.C: A crescendo-decrescendo ejection murmur occurs in systole, as in aortic stenosis, not after S2.

The other points (A=aortic, P=pulmonary, T=tricuspid, M=mitral) localize their respective valve sounds.

questions.stem: This short-axis gross section of the ventricles shows a markedly thickened left-sided chamber wall. What does this specimen demonstrate?

explanation.whyCorrect: The left ventricular free wall and septum are conspicuously thicker than the right ventricular wall, indicating left ventricular hypertrophy. This is a chronic adaptation to increased LV workload, as in hypertension or aortic valve disease.

questions.stem: This intraoperative view of an infant heart shows a domed, fused pulmonary valve creating a narrowed outflow orifice above the right ventricle. What chronic cardiac adaptation does this obstruction impose?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Left ventricular dilation from volume overload

choices.label: B
choices.text: Right ventricular hypertrophy from pressure overload

choices.label: D
choices.text: Left atrial enlargement from mitral regurgitation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Right atrial thinning from tricuspid regurgitation

explanation.summary: Congenital pulmonary valve stenosis with fused commissures obstructs right ventricular outflow. The RV must generate higher systolic pressure to eject across the narrowed valve, and chronic pressure overload leads to concentric right ventricular hypertrophy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Congenital pulmonary valve stenosis with fused commissures obstructs right ventricular outflow. The RV must generate higher systolic pressure to eject across the narrowed valve, and chronic pressure overload leads to concentric right ventricular hypertrophy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Pulmonary stenosis loads the right ventricle, not the left, and causes pressure rather than volume overload.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Global dilation is the pattern of dilated cardiomyopathy, not the response to outflow obstruction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Left atrial enlargement from mitral regurgitation is a left-sided lesion, unrelated to a stenotic pulmonary valve.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tricuspid regurgitation enlarges the right atrium rather than thinning it, and is not the primary consequence of pulmonary stenosis.

questions.topicName: Aortic Regurgitation and Pulmonary Valve Disease
questions.stem: This illustration shows a proximal (type A) aortic dissection whose flap disrupts the aortic valve leaflet alignment. If this produces acute severe aortic regurgitation, what is the most immediate life-threatening consequence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Systemic hypertension with a widened pulse pressure over months

choices.label: B
choices.text: Gradual, well-tolerated LV dilation over many years

choices.label: C
choices.text: Acute pulmonary edema and cardiogenic shock

choices.label: D
choices.text: Isolated right-heart failure with peripheral edema

explanation.summary: In acute aortic regurgitation the left ventricle has not had time to dilate, so it cannot buffer the regurgitant volume. LV end-diastolic pressure rises sharply, transmitting back to the lungs and causing acute pulmonary edema and cardiogenic shock, a surgical emergency, unlike the well-tolerated chronic form.
explanation.whyCorrect: In acute aortic regurgitation the left ventricle has not had time to dilate, so it cannot buffer the regurgitant volume. LV end-diastolic pressure rises sharply, transmitting back to the lungs and causing acute pulmonary edema and cardiogenic shock, a surgical emergency, unlike the well-tolerated chronic form.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Widened pulse pressure developing over months reflects chronic aortic regurgitation, not the acute catastrophic form.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Gradual, well-tolerated dilation describes chronic regurgitation; acute regurgitation gives no time for adaptation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Acute aortic regurgitation backs pressure into the left atrium and lungs, not isolated right-heart failure.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Compensated eccentric hypertrophy takes months to years and is the adaptation of chronic, not acute, regurgitation.

questions.topicName: Aortic Regurgitation and Pulmonary Valve Disease
questions.stem: The lower pathway shows sarcomeres added in series with a dilated, thin-walled ventricle, contrasting with the middle pathway. Which hemodynamic burden classically drives the lower (eccentric) pattern?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chronic pressure overload from systemic hypertension

choices.label: E
choices.text: Acute pressure overload from aortic stenosis

explanation.summary: Adding sarcomeres in series lengthens myocytes, producing eccentric hypertrophy with chamber dilation, the response to chronic volume overload. Adding sarcomeres in parallel thickens myocytes, producing concentric hypertrophy in response to pressure overload.
explanation.whyCorrect: Adding sarcomeres in series lengthens myocytes, producing eccentric hypertrophy with chamber dilation, the response to chronic volume overload. Adding sarcomeres in parallel thickens myocytes, producing concentric hypertrophy in response to pressure overload.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chronic pressure overload adds sarcomeres in parallel and produces concentric hypertrophy, the middle pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Acute coronary occlusion causes infarction and regional dysfunction, not series sarcomere addition.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pericardial constriction limits filling and does not drive eccentric hypertrophy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Aortic stenosis is a pressure load that produces concentric hypertrophy, and it is typically chronic rather than acute.

questions.topicName: Aortic Regurgitation and Pulmonary Valve Disease
questions.stem: Using the Laplace relationship shown (T = P·r / 2h), what is the functional purpose of the increased wall thickness (h) that develops in concentric hypertrophy during pressure overload?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Increasing wall thickness has no effect on wall tension

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increasing wall thickness reduces the intraventricular pressure directly

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increasing wall thickness enlarges the chamber radius

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increasing wall thickness raises wall tension to boost contraction

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increasing wall thickness lowers wall tension back toward normal

explanation.summary: By the law of Laplace, wall tension is proportional to pressure times radius and inversely proportional to wall thickness. In pressure overload, thickening the wall (increased h) offsets the increased pressure so that tension is normalized. In volume overload, the radius rises and eccentric hypertrophy predominates.
explanation.whyCorrect: By the law of Laplace, wall tension is proportional to pressure times radius and inversely proportional to wall thickness. In pressure overload, thickening the wall (increased h) offsets the increased pressure so that tension is normalized. In volume overload, the radius rises and eccentric hypertrophy predominates.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Wall thickness appears in the denominator of the Laplace relationship, so it directly reduces wall tension.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Thickening the wall does not lower ventricular pressure; it distributes that pressure across more muscle to lower stress.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Concentric thickening maintains or reduces cavity size; radius enlargement is the hallmark of volume overload.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Greater thickness lowers wall tension, which is the adaptive purpose in pressure overload.

choices.label: E

whyWrongByChoice.B: Aortic regurgitation loads the left ventricle; right ventricular hypertrophy reflects pulmonary pressure overload.

questions.topicName: Aortic Regurgitation and Pulmonary Valve Disease
questions.stem: Compared with the normal aortic root and valve on the left, the right side shows a widened root in which the leaflets no longer meet in the center. Which mechanism of aortic regurgitation does this illustrate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Rheumatic thickening and fusion of the leaflets

choices.label: C
choices.text: A bacterial vegetation perforating a cusp

choices.label: D
choices.text: Congenital fusion into a bicuspid valve

explanation.summary: Even with structurally intact leaflets, dilation of the aortic root and annulus pulls the cusps apart so they cannot coapt during diastole, producing regurgitation. This is the mechanism seen in aortic root aneurysm, Marfan syndrome, and dissection, as opposed to primary leaflet disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Even with structurally intact leaflets, dilation of the aortic root and annulus pulls the cusps apart so they cannot coapt during diastole, producing regurgitation. This is the mechanism seen in aortic root aneurysm, Marfan syndrome, and dissection, as opposed to primary leaflet disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Rheumatic disease thickens and fuses the leaflets themselves, whereas here the leaflets are intact but pulled apart by the dilated root.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Calcific stenosis restricts leaflet opening and causes obstruction, not failure of central coaptation from root widening.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A vegetation perforating a cusp damages the leaflet itself, which is not the mechanism shown with a widened root.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A bicuspid valve has two leaflets of abnormal structure, whereas the figure shows normal leaflets separated by root dilation.

questions.stem: This left ventricular pressure-volume loop (shifted rightward with a very large stroke-volume width and high end-diastolic volume) together with the arterial tracing showing a large pulse pressure is characteristic of which valvular lesion?

explanation.summary: Chronic aortic regurgitation produces combined volume and pressure overload: the PV loop enlarges with a greatly increased end-diastolic volume and stroke volume, while diastolic runoff of blood back into the LV lowers diastolic aortic pressure, widening the pulse pressure.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chronic aortic regurgitation produces combined volume and pressure overload: the PV loop enlarges with a greatly increased end-diastolic volume and stroke volume, while diastolic runoff of blood back into the LV lowers diastolic aortic pressure, widening the pulse pressure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acute mitral regurgitation gives a loop with no true isovolumetric contraction and a normal or narrow pulse pressure, without a chronically huge end-diastolic volume.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Constrictive pericarditis limits filling, producing a small loop with reduced end-diastolic volume.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mitral stenosis underfills the left ventricle, giving a small loop with low end-diastolic volume.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Aortic stenosis produces a tall loop with high systolic pressure and normal or reduced stroke volume, not a wide pulse pressure.

questions.topicName: Aortic Regurgitation and Pulmonary Valve Disease
questions.stem: This curve plots stroke volume against ventricular end-diastolic volume. Which physiological principle does it illustrate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Bowditch (treppe) effect of rate on contractility

choices.label: B
choices.text: Anrep effect of afterload on intrinsic contractility

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Bainbridge reflex increasing heart rate with venous return

choices.label: E
choices.text: Laplace's law relating wall tension to radius and pressure

explanation.summary: As end-diastolic volume (preload) rises, sarcomere stretch optimizes actin-myosin overlap so stroke volume increases, peaking around ~170 mL before declining with overstretch. This is the Frank-Starling relationship.
explanation.whyCorrect: As end-diastolic volume (preload) rises, sarcomere stretch optimizes actin-myosin overlap so stroke volume increases, peaking around ~170 mL before declining with overstretch. This is the Frank-Starling relationship.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The Bowditch (treppe) effect describes contractility rising with heart rate; it would be plotted against rate, not against end-diastolic volume.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The Anrep effect is a slow rise in intrinsic contractility after an abrupt increase in afterload; this curve varies preload, not afterload.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The Bainbridge reflex is an atrial stretch reflex that raises heart rate with increased venous return; it changes rate, not stroke volume as a function of EDV.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Laplace's law relates wall tension to chamber pressure, radius and wall thickness; it does not describe stroke volume rising with end-diastolic volume.

questions.topicName: Acute Rheumatic Fever and Rheumatic Heart Disease
questions.stem: This H&E-stained myocardium shows an interstitial focus of collagen degeneration surrounded by mononuclear cells with slender, ribbon-like ('caterpillar') nuclei. The presence of this lesion is most specifically diagnostic of which condition?

explanation.summary: The central focus is an Aschoff body, and the caterpillar-nuclei macrophages are Anitschkow cells. Aschoff bodies with Anitschkow cells are the pathognomonic myocardial lesion of rheumatic carditis, a delayed autoimmune sequela of group A streptococcal pharyngitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The central focus is an Aschoff body, and the caterpillar-nuclei macrophages are Anitschkow cells. Aschoff bodies with Anitschkow cells are the pathognomonic myocardial lesion of rheumatic carditis, a delayed autoimmune sequela of group A streptococcal pharyngitis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Amyloid cardiomyopathy shows extracellular pink amorphous deposits with apple-green birefringence on Congo red, not granulomatous foci with caterpillar-nucleus macrophages.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Coxsackievirus myocarditis produces a diffuse lymphocytic infiltrate with myocyte necrosis, without the organized collagen-centered nodules of Aschoff bodies.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Acute infarction shows coagulative necrosis followed by neutrophils and later granulation tissue in a vascular territory, not interstitial granulomas with Anitschkow cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sarcoidosis forms well-formed non-caseating granulomas with epithelioid histiocytes and multinucleated giant cells, not fibrinoid collagen foci rimmed by caterpillar cells.

questions.topicName: Acute Rheumatic Fever and Rheumatic Heart Disease
questions.stem: This high-power histologic field from inflamed myocardium highlights plump macrophages whose central chromatin forms a slender, wavy ribbon resembling a caterpillar. What are these cells called?

explanation.summary: Anitschkow cells are activated macrophages with a characteristic central bar of chromatin giving a caterpillar (or owl-eye in cross-section) appearance. They aggregate within Aschoff bodies and are a histologic hallmark of rheumatic carditis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Anitschkow cells are activated macrophages with a characteristic central bar of chromatin giving a caterpillar (or owl-eye in cross-section) appearance. They aggregate within Aschoff bodies and are a histologic hallmark of rheumatic carditis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Foam cells are macrophages with abundant bubbly, lipid-filled cytoplasm, seen in atheromas and xanthomas; their nuclei are not ribbon-like bars.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Langhans giant cells are multinucleated cells with nuclei arranged in a horseshoe at the periphery, typical of tuberculous and other granulomas.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reed-Sternberg cells are large binucleate or bilobed B-cell-derived cells with owl-eye nucleoli, found in Hodgkin lymphoma, not myocardium.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Touton giant cells have a wreath of nuclei surrounded by foamy cytoplasm and occur in xanthogranulomatous lesions, not rheumatic carditis.

questions.topicName: Acute Rheumatic Fever and Rheumatic Heart Disease
questions.stem: This Gram stain of the organism that triggers rheumatic fever shows purple-staining cocci arranged in long chains. Which organism is this?

explanation.whyCorrect: Group A Streptococcus (S. pyogenes) is a gram-positive coccus in chains; pharyngitis with this organism triggers the immune cross-reaction that causes acute rheumatic fever.

whyWrongByChoice.E: Staphylococcus aureus forms gram-positive cocci in grape-like clusters, not chains, and is not linked to rheumatic fever.

questions.topicName: Acute Rheumatic Fever and Rheumatic Heart Disease
questions.stem: This patient with a recent streptococcal infection develops a pink, non-pruritic, serpiginous rash with central clearing over the limb. What is this skin finding?

explanation.whyCorrect: Erythema marginatum — an evanescent, annular rash with central clearing over the trunk and proximal limbs — is a major Jones criterion for acute rheumatic fever.

whyWrongByChoice.C: Erythema multiforme produces fixed target lesions with dusky centers, typically after HSV or drugs, rather than evanescent rings with central clearing.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Necrolytic migratory erythema is a crusting, erosive migratory rash of the groin and perineum seen with glucagonoma, unrelated to streptococcal infection.

questions.topicName: Acute Rheumatic Fever and Rheumatic Heart Disease
questions.stem: This opened left heart from a patient with a history of childhood rheumatic fever shows a thickened valve and a hypertrophied ventricle. Repeated rheumatic inflammation of this valve most characteristically produces which lesion?

explanation.summary: Chronic rheumatic heart disease most often scars the mitral valve, fusing the commissures and thickening the leaflets to produce mitral stenosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chronic rheumatic heart disease most often scars the mitral valve, fusing the commissures and thickening the leaflets to produce mitral stenosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Rheumatic disease can involve the aortic valve, but almost always together with the mitral valve; isolated aortic stenosis is usually calcific or bicuspid.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Tricuspid involvement in rheumatic disease is uncommon, and tricuspid regurgitation is more often functional from right ventricular dilation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mitral valve prolapse results from myxomatous degeneration with redundant leaflets, not the fibrosis and commissural fusion of chronic rheumatic disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pulmonary stenosis is almost always congenital and is rarely, if ever, a result of rheumatic valvulitis.

questions.topicName: Acute Rheumatic Fever and Rheumatic Heart Disease
questions.stem: This view into the left atrium shows diffusely thickened, fused mitral leaflets narrowing the orifice into a slit. What is the classic descriptive term for this deformity?

explanation.summary: Chronic rheumatic mitral stenosis fuses the commissures and thickens the leaflets, narrowing the orifice into the characteristic 'fish-mouth' or 'buttonhole' opening.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chronic rheumatic mitral stenosis fuses the commissures and thickens the leaflets, narrowing the orifice into the characteristic 'fish-mouth' or 'buttonhole' opening.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A congenital bicuspid valve is an aortic valve with two cusps, a developmental anomaly rather than acquired fusion of mitral leaflets.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Myxomatous degeneration produces thin, redundant, billowing leaflets that prolapse, the opposite of thickened, fused, narrowed leaflets.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Endocarditis vegetations are friable masses on the leaflets that destroy tissue; they do not fuse commissures into a slit-like orifice.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A flail leaflet results from chordal rupture, letting a leaflet tip evert into the atrium and causing regurgitation, not a narrowed orifice.

choices.label: C

choices.label: D

explanation.whyCorrect: The device is an annuloplasty ring. It is sewn around a dilated mitral annulus to shrink and reshape it, allowing the native leaflets to coapt again and thereby correcting regurgitation while preserving the patient's own valve.

questions.topicName: Mitral Regurgitation and Mitral Valve Prolapse
questions.stem: This diagram labels the components of a heart valve, including the anterior annulus, anterior leaflet, chordae tendineae, and papillary muscles. Which valve's apparatus is depicted?

questions.topicName: Mitral Regurgitation and Mitral Valve Prolapse
questions.stem: This histologic section of a mitral leaflet shows the fibrosa, an irregularly thickened spongiosa layer, and the atrialis. Which valvular disorder does this expanded, disorganized spongiosa indicate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Amyloid infiltration of the valve stroma

choices.label: C
choices.text: Myxomatous degeneration causing mitral valve prolapse

explanation.summary: Accumulation of proteoglycan-rich ground substance expands the spongiosa and fragments the fibrosa, weakening the leaflet. This myxomatous (myxoid) degeneration produces the redundant, floppy leaflets of mitral valve prolapse.
explanation.whyCorrect: Accumulation of proteoglycan-rich ground substance expands the spongiosa and fragments the fibrosa, weakening the leaflet. This myxomatous (myxoid) degeneration produces the redundant, floppy leaflets of mitral valve prolapse.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Amyloid infiltration deposits amorphous eosinophilic material throughout the stroma, not a selectively expanded, proteoglycan-rich spongiosa.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Rheumatic valvulitis causes fibrosis, neovascularization and commissural fusion, thickening the leaflet with scar rather than myxoid ground substance.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Infective endocarditis produces surface vegetations of fibrin, platelets, and organisms with leaflet destruction, not internal expansion of the spongiosa.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Calcific degeneration deposits basophilic calcium nodules, typically in the fibrosa or annulus, rather than loose myxoid material in the spongiosa.

questions.topicName: Mitral Regurgitation and Mitral Valve Prolapse
questions.stem: This parasternal long-axis echocardiogram shows systolic billowing of the mitral leaflets more than 2 mm above the annular plane (red line). What auscultatory finding is classically associated with this condition?

explanation.summary: Displacement of redundant myxomatous leaflets above the annulus defines mitral valve prolapse, which produces a mid-systolic click (often followed by a late systolic murmur if regurgitation is present).
explanation.whyCorrect: Displacement of redundant myxomatous leaflets above the annulus defines mitral valve prolapse, which produces a mid-systolic click (often followed by a late systolic murmur if regurgitation is present).

whyWrongByChoice.A: A pericardial friction rub is a scratchy three-component sound of pericarditis, unrelated to mitral leaflet prolapse.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fixed splitting of S2 is the hallmark of an atrial septal defect, not of a myxomatous mitral valve.
whyWrongByChoice.D: An opening snap is an early diastolic sound from stiff, stenotic mitral leaflets, not a systolic sound from billowing leaflets.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An S3 reflects rapid early diastolic filling of a volume-overloaded or failing ventricle and is not the classic finding of prolapse.

questions.topicName: Mitral Regurgitation and Mitral Valve Prolapse
questions.stem: This opened heart shows a mitral valve with fibrotic, thickened, fused leaflets narrowing the orifice. What auscultatory finding is most expected from this lesion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Opening snap followed by a diastolic rumble

explanation.summary: Leaflet fibrosis, thickening, and commissural fusion produce mitral stenosis, which classically causes an opening snap and a low-pitched mid-diastolic rumble; a holosystolic murmur would indicate regurgitation instead.
explanation.whyCorrect: Leaflet fibrosis, thickening, and commissural fusion produce mitral stenosis, which classically causes an opening snap and a low-pitched mid-diastolic rumble; a holosystolic murmur would indicate regurgitation instead.

whyWrongByChoice.C: A continuous machine-like murmur is typical of a patent ductus arteriosus, spanning systole and diastole.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A crescendo-decrescendo systolic ejection murmur is characteristic of aortic stenosis, not obstruction at the mitral orifice.

questions.topicName: Mitral Regurgitation and Mitral Valve Prolapse
questions.stem: This explanted valve shows thickened leaflets with fusion at the commissures (arrows). What is the most common underlying etiology worldwide for this valvular deformity?

explanation.summary: Commissural fusion with leaflet and chordal thickening producing a fish-mouth orifice is the hallmark of chronic rheumatic valvulitis, the leading cause of mitral stenosis worldwide.
explanation.whyCorrect: Commissural fusion with leaflet and chordal thickening producing a fish-mouth orifice is the hallmark of chronic rheumatic valvulitis, the leading cause of mitral stenosis worldwide.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Infective endocarditis destroys and perforates leaflets with vegetations; it does not typically cause symmetric commissural fusion.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A bicuspid malformation affects the aortic valve and is a congenital two-cusp structure, not acquired fusion with leaflet thickening.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Myxomatous degeneration creates floppy, redundant leaflets that prolapse, without commissural fusion or stenosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Carcinoid heart disease causes plaque-like fibrosis mainly of right-sided valves (tricuspid and pulmonary) and is rare compared with rheumatic disease.

questions.topicName: Mitral Regurgitation and Mitral Valve Prolapse
questions.stem: These two illustrations show a chorda tendinea rupture and a papillary muscle rupture affecting the mitral apparatus. What clinical presentation do these mechanisms most characteristically cause?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Slowly progressive tricuspid regurgitation with peripheral edema

choices.label: B
choices.text: Gradual aortic regurgitation with a wide pulse pressure

choices.label: C
choices.text: Acute severe mitral regurgitation with sudden pulmonary edema

choices.label: D
choices.text: Asymptomatic mid-systolic click without hemodynamic effect

choices.label: E
choices.text: Chronic compensated mitral stenosis with atrial enlargement

explanation.summary: Rupture of a chorda or papillary muscle (classically a few days after inferior MI) abruptly deprives a leaflet of support, causing acute severe mitral regurgitation. Because the atrium and pulmonary vasculature have no time to adapt, patients present with sudden flash pulmonary edema and hypotension.
explanation.whyCorrect: Rupture of a chorda or papillary muscle (classically a few days after inferior MI) abruptly deprives a leaflet of support, causing acute severe mitral regurgitation. Because the atrium and pulmonary vasculature have no time to adapt, patients present with sudden flash pulmonary edema and hypotension.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chordal and papillary muscle rupture shown here involves the mitral apparatus, and its onset is abrupt, not a slowly progressive right-sided lesion.
whyWrongByChoice.B: These mechanisms affect the mitral valve, not the aortic valve; a wide pulse pressure is the sign of chronic aortic regurgitation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: An isolated mid-systolic click is the benign finding of mitral valve prolapse; loss of leaflet support produces severe, hemodynamically significant regurgitation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Loss of chordal support makes a leaflet flail and leak, causing regurgitation rather than stenosis, and the presentation is acute, not chronic.

questions.topicName: Mitral Regurgitation and Mitral Valve Prolapse
questions.stem: This cardiac diagram depicts asymmetric septal thickening with a high-velocity outflow jet and a posteriorly directed mitral regurgitant jet. What mechanism directly causes the mitral regurgitation shown?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve

explanation.summary: In hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, the hypertrophied septum accelerates outflow, drawing the anterior mitral leaflet toward the septum (systolic anterior motion), which obstructs outflow and creates a posteriorly directed regurgitant jet.
explanation.whyCorrect: In hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, the hypertrophied septum accelerates outflow, drawing the anterior mitral leaflet toward the septum (systolic anterior motion), which obstructs outflow and creates a posteriorly directed regurgitant jet.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ruptured chordae produce a flail leaflet with acute regurgitation, but the diagram shows a hypertrophied septum dragging an intact leaflet into the outflow tract.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Annular calcification is a degenerative process of the elderly that impairs annular contraction, unrelated to septal hypertrophy and outflow obstruction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Papillary muscle infarction follows myocardial infarction and causes acute regurgitation, not the dynamic outflow-related leak of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Endocarditis vegetations destroy leaflet tissue in the setting of infection; nothing in a hypertrophied, obstructed ventricle points to that.

questions.topicName: Mitral Regurgitation and Mitral Valve Prolapse
questions.stem: This left ventricular pressure-volume loop compares the normal loop with that of chronic mitral regurgitation. What key hemodynamic change does the regurgitant loop demonstrate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A prolonged isovolumetric relaxation phase with normal volumes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased end-diastolic volume with a larger total stroke volume

choices.label: C
choices.text: Elevated afterload with a tall, narrow loop

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reduced end-diastolic volume with a narrow stroke volume

explanation.summary: In chronic MR the incompetent valve allows systolic backflow, so there is no true isovolumetric contraction; volume overload raises LVEDV and total (forward plus regurgitant) stroke volume, widening and right-shifting the loop.
explanation.whyCorrect: In chronic MR the incompetent valve allows systolic backflow, so there is no true isovolumetric contraction; volume overload raises LVEDV and total (forward plus regurgitant) stroke volume, widening and right-shifting the loop.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chronic mitral regurgitation actually removes a true isovolumetric phase because the valve leaks; it does not leave volumes normal.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A tall, narrow loop reflects pressure overload such as aortic stenosis, whereas regurgitation produces a wide, right-shifted loop.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Volume overload from regurgitant flow increases, not decreases, end-diastolic volume and total stroke volume.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Preload is increased in chronic mitral regurgitation because regurgitant blood returns to the ventricle in diastole.

questions.topicName: Mitral Regurgitation and Mitral Valve Prolapse
questions.stem: These two phonocardiogram tracings contrast murmurs occurring between S1 and S2. What feature distinguishes the lower (mitral regurgitation) tracing from the upper (aortic stenosis) tracing?

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a mid-diastolic rumble after an opening snap

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a continuous murmur spanning S2

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is an early diastolic decrescendo murmur

explanation.whyCorrect: Mitral regurgitation produces a uniform-intensity holosystolic murmur because the pressure gradient between LV and LA is constant throughout systole, whereas aortic stenosis produces a crescendo-decrescendo ejection murmur that tapers before S2.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A mid-diastolic rumble after an opening snap is the sound of mitral stenosis, which occurs in diastole, not between S1 and S2.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A continuous murmur spanning S2 is characteristic of a patent ductus arteriosus, not mitral regurgitation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Both tracings lie between S1 and S2, so the regurgitant murmur is systolic; a purely diastolic murmur would be stenosis or aortic regurgitation.

questions.topicName: Mitral Regurgitation and Mitral Valve Prolapse
questions.stem: This phonocardiogram diagram shows the midsystolic click and late systolic murmur of mitral valve prolapse and how they shift after sudden standing versus sudden squatting. What accounts for the click and murmur occurring EARLIER after sudden standing?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased venous return reduces LV volume

choices.label: B
choices.text: Elevated left atrial pressure prevents the leaflets from prolapsing

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bradycardia lengthens diastole and shifts the murmur toward S1

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased LV filling stretches the chordae and abolishes the click

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increased afterload delays leaflet coaptation, moving the click later

explanation.summary: Standing decreases preload and LV end-diastolic volume; the smaller ventricle allows the redundant leaflet to prolapse sooner, moving the click and murmur closer to S1. Squatting increases preload and afterload, enlarging the LV and delaying the click toward S2.
explanation.whyCorrect: Standing decreases preload and LV end-diastolic volume; the smaller ventricle allows the redundant leaflet to prolapse sooner, moving the click and murmur closer to S1. Squatting increases preload and afterload, enlarging the LV and delaying the click toward S2.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Left atrial pressure does not prevent prolapse; the timing of the click depends on LV size, which shrinks with the fall in preload on standing.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Standing produces a reflex tachycardia, not bradycardia, and diastolic length does not determine when a systolic click occurs.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Increased LV filling occurs with squatting, which delays the click; standing reduces filling.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Afterload does not rise meaningfully on standing, and moving the click later is the effect of squatting, the opposite of what is asked.

questions.topicName: Mitral Regurgitation and Mitral Valve Prolapse
questions.stem: This diagram contrasts a normal mitral valve with a regurgitant one during ventricular systole. What is the direct hemodynamic consequence of the abnormality shown on the right?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blood regurgitates from the aorta back into the left ventricle

choices.label: B
choices.text: Blood is obstructed as it enters the left ventricle during diastole

choices.label: C
choices.text: Blood flows backward from the left ventricle into the left atrium during systole

choices.label: D
choices.text: Blood pools in the pulmonary veins without entering the atrium

choices.label: E
choices.text: Blood shunts from the left atrium to the right atrium

explanation.summary: When the mitral leaflets fail to coapt during systole, a portion of the LV stroke volume is ejected retrograde into the left atrium instead of forward into the aorta, producing the holosystolic murmur and volume overload of mitral regurgitation.
explanation.whyCorrect: When the mitral leaflets fail to coapt during systole, a portion of the LV stroke volume is ejected retrograde into the left atrium instead of forward into the aorta, producing the holosystolic murmur and volume overload of mitral regurgitation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Backflow from the aorta into the ventricle is aortic regurgitation and occurs in diastole, not mitral leaflet failure in systole.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Obstruction of ventricular inflow in diastole describes mitral stenosis, not leaflets that fail to close during systole.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pulmonary venous congestion can result secondarily, but blood is not prevented from entering the atrium; the direct problem is retrograde flow into it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Left-to-right atrial shunting requires an atrial septal defect, which is not part of a regurgitant mitral valve.

questions.topicName: Mitral Regurgitation and Mitral Valve Prolapse
questions.stem: This diagram contrasts a normal left ventricle with one in which the papillary muscle is displaced, the leaflets are tethered, and closure is restricted. What type of mitral regurgitation does this mechanism represent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Primary regurgitation from a torn, flail leaflet

choices.label: C
choices.text: Regurgitation from infective vegetations destroying the cusp

choices.label: D
choices.text: Congenital regurgitation from a cleft anterior leaflet

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rheumatic regurgitation from commissural fusion and thickening

explanation.whyCorrect: When ventricular dilation displaces the papillary muscles outward, the chordae tether otherwise normal leaflets and prevent full closure. This is functional (secondary) mitral regurgitation, driven by ventricular geometry rather than intrinsic valve disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Primary regurgitation from a flail leaflet involves an intrinsically damaged valve with chordal tear, whereas here the leaflets are normal but tethered.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Vegetations destroy leaflet tissue in endocarditis, an intrinsic valve lesion unrelated to papillary muscle displacement.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A cleft anterior leaflet is a congenital defect, often with an AV canal defect, not an acquired consequence of ventricular remodeling.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Rheumatic disease thickens and fuses leaflets intrinsically, whereas this mechanism leaves the leaflets normal and pulls them apart.

questions.topicName: Tricuspid Regurgitation and Tricuspid Stenosis
questions.stem: In the abnormal heart shown, the tricuspid valve is elongated and displaced apically into the right ventricle. What is the chief functional consequence of this displacement?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Aortic root dilation with aortic regurgitation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fixed diastolic obstruction of right ventricular inflow

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reversal of flow across a patent ductus arteriosus

explanation.summary: Apical displacement of the septal/posterior tricuspid leaflets makes the valve leak backward into the right atrium and incorporates the inflow portion of the RV into a functional (atrialized) chamber, reducing effective RV volume; an associated atrial septal defect permits right-to-left shunting.
explanation.whyCorrect: Apical displacement of the septal/posterior tricuspid leaflets makes the valve leak backward into the right atrium and incorporates the inflow portion of the RV into a functional (atrialized) chamber, reducing effective RV volume; an associated atrial septal defect permits right-to-left shunting.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The displaced valve is the tricuspid on the right side, so it does not obstruct left ventricular outflow.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Aortic root dilation with regurgitation is a feature of Marfan syndrome or bicuspid aortopathy, not apical displacement of the tricuspid valve.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ebstein anomaly causes a leaky, incompetent tricuspid valve; fixed inflow obstruction is the picture of tricuspid stenosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Flow reversal across a ductus reflects pulmonary hypertension (Eisenmenger physiology), not the primary consequence of a displaced tricuspid valve.

questions.stem: These three panels (normal, annular dilation, and papillary muscle displacement) illustrate the mechanisms behind which category of tricuspid regurgitation?

explanation.summary: Functional/secondary TR occurs with structurally normal leaflets that fail to coapt because of tricuspid annular dilation and/or apical tethering of the leaflets from papillary muscle displacement, typically driven by right ventricular or right atrial remodeling.
explanation.whyCorrect: Functional/secondary TR occurs with structurally normal leaflets that fail to coapt because of tricuspid annular dilation and/or apical tethering of the leaflets from papillary muscle displacement, typically driven by right ventricular or right atrial remodeling.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Endocarditis causes primary leaflet destruction or perforation, whereas these panels show intact leaflets pulled apart by annular and papillary changes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Carcinoid disease thickens and retracts the leaflets themselves (primary disease), not the annulus or papillary muscle geometry.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ebstein anomaly is a congenital apical displacement of the leaflets themselves, not acquired annular dilation or tethering.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Rheumatic involvement causes primary leaflet thickening and fusion, the opposite category from the normal-leaflet mechanisms shown.

questions.topicName: Tricuspid Regurgitation and Tricuspid Stenosis
questions.stem: In the lower jugular venous pressure tracing, the normal separate C and V waves are replaced by a single large fused 'CV' wave with loss of the X descent. What mechanism produces this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Complete atrioventricular dissociation with cannon waves

choices.label: B
choices.text: Pericardial constriction limiting late diastolic filling

choices.label: C
choices.text: Impaired atrial emptying across a stenosed valve during diastole

choices.label: D
choices.text: Loss of atrial contraction from atrial fibrillation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Regurgitant flow from the right ventricle into the right atrium

explanation.summary: In tricuspid regurgitation, systolic backflow into the right atrium abolishes the normal systolic X descent and fuses the c and v waves into a giant 'CV' (or 's') wave, a hallmark of the JVP in TR.
explanation.whyCorrect: In tricuspid regurgitation, systolic backflow into the right atrium abolishes the normal systolic X descent and fuses the c and v waves into a giant 'CV' (or 's') wave, a hallmark of the JVP in TR.

whyWrongByChoice.A: AV dissociation produces intermittent cannon a waves when the atrium contracts against a closed valve, not a fused systolic CV wave.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Constriction produces a prominent, steep Y descent (and often X descent), not loss of the X descent with a fused systolic wave.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Impaired atrial emptying across a stenotic valve gives a giant a wave and slow Y descent, which is tricuspid stenosis, not a fused CV wave.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Atrial fibrillation abolishes the a wave, but the systolic X descent loss and giant CV wave require regurgitant systolic flow.

questions.topicName: Tricuspid Regurgitation and Tricuspid Stenosis
questions.stem: The right-hand heart diagram differs from the normal by a thickened, narrowed tricuspid orifice. What is the primary hemodynamic consequence of this lesion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Obstructed diastolic flow from the right atrium to right ventricle

choices.label: B
choices.text: Left-to-right shunting through an atrial septal defect

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased pulmonary arterial pressure from left ventricular failure

choices.label: E
choices.text: Systolic backflow from the right ventricle into the right atrium

explanation.summary: Tricuspid stenosis restricts diastolic filling of the right ventricle, creating a diastolic pressure gradient across the valve and elevating right atrial pressure. This produces systemic venous congestion (hepatomegaly, ascites, edema) and a prominent a wave in the JVP.
explanation.whyCorrect: Tricuspid stenosis restricts diastolic filling of the right ventricle, creating a diastolic pressure gradient across the valve and elevating right atrial pressure. This produces systemic venous congestion (hepatomegaly, ascites, edema) and a prominent a wave in the JVP.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A narrowed tricuspid orifice does not create an atrial septal defect; left-to-right atrial shunting requires a septal opening.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pulmonary hypertension from left heart failure arises upstream of the left heart, not from obstruction at the tricuspid valve.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reduced aortic outflow in systole describes aortic stenosis; tricuspid narrowing impairs diastolic right heart filling.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Systolic backflow into the right atrium is tricuspid regurgitation, which occurs with an incompetent, not a narrowed, valve.

questions.topicName: Tricuspid Regurgitation and Tricuspid Stenosis
questions.stem: Compared with the normal tracing, the lower jugular venous waveform shows a tall/prominent A wave and a slow, blunted Y descent. What underlies these changes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Systolic regurgitation abolishing the X descent

choices.label: B
choices.text: Forceful atrial contraction against, and impaired atrial emptying through, a stenotic tricuspid valve

choices.label: C
choices.text: Rapid ventricular filling from constrictive pericarditis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cannon a waves from atrioventricular dissociation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Loss of organized atrial activity in atrial fibrillation

explanation.summary: In tricuspid stenosis the right atrium contracts vigorously against the obstructed valve, producing a giant a wave, while the narrowed orifice slows diastolic emptying, blunting and prolonging the y descent.
explanation.whyCorrect: In tricuspid stenosis the right atrium contracts vigorously against the obstructed valve, producing a giant a wave, while the narrowed orifice slows diastolic emptying, blunting and prolonging the y descent.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Systolic regurgitation would erase the X descent and create a giant CV wave, not a tall a wave with slow Y descent.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Constrictive pericarditis gives a rapid, steep Y descent from early diastolic filling, the opposite of the blunted Y shown.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cannon a waves are intermittent and irregular from AV dissociation, whereas this a wave is consistently tall with a slow Y descent.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Atrial fibrillation eliminates organized atrial contraction, so the a wave would be absent rather than prominent.

questions.topicName: Mitral Stenosis
questions.stem: This labeled diagram shows leaflets anchored by chordae tendineae to papillary muscles, with an anterior leaflet and anterior annulus. Which structure normally prevents these leaflets from everting into the atrium during systole?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The moderator band bracing the free wall

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chordae tendineae anchoring the leaflets to the papillary muscles

choices.label: C
choices.text: The trabeculae carneae lining the ventricular apex

choices.label: D
choices.text: The interventricular septum pushing the leaflets shut

choices.label: E
choices.text: The annular ring contracting to seal the orifice

explanation.summary: During systole the papillary muscles contract and the chordae tendineae hold the mitral leaflets in a closed position, preventing them from prolapsing back into the left atrium. Failure of this apparatus (e.g., chordal rupture) leads to regurgitation.
explanation.whyCorrect: During systole the papillary muscles contract and the chordae tendineae hold the mitral leaflets in a closed position, preventing them from prolapsing back into the left atrium. Failure of this apparatus (e.g., chordal rupture) leads to regurgitation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The moderator band is a muscular bridge in the right ventricle carrying the right bundle branch; it does not tether leaflets.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The trabeculae carneae are irregular muscular ridges of the ventricular wall and have no direct attachment to valve leaflets.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The septum does not push the leaflets closed; closure is driven by the ventricular pressure gradient and restrained by chordae.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The annulus does contract slightly in systole, but it cannot stop the leaflet edges from everting into the atrium.

questions.topicName: Mitral Stenosis
questions.stem: This cadaveric atrial-view photograph shows a large anterior leaflet, a scalloped posterior leaflet (P1-P3 segments), and anterolateral and posteromedial commissures. Which cardiac valve is displayed?

explanation.summary: The bileaflet arrangement with a single broad anterior leaflet, a scalloped three-segment posterior leaflet, and two commissures is the hallmark surgical anatomy of the mitral valve viewed from the left atrium.
explanation.whyCorrect: The bileaflet arrangement with a single broad anterior leaflet, a scalloped three-segment posterior leaflet, and two commissures is the hallmark surgical anatomy of the mitral valve viewed from the left atrium.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The aortic valve has three semilunar cusps named for the coronary ostia, not anterior and scalloped posterior leaflets.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The pulmonary valve is a three-cusp semilunar valve with no anterior or scalloped posterior leaflet.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The tricuspid valve has three leaflets (anterior, septal, posterior) and is not described with P1-P3 scallops or anterolateral and posteromedial commissures.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The coronary sinus ostium is an opening in the right atrium, not a valve with leaflets and commissures.

questions.stem: This diagram shows a catheter advanced from the inferior vena cava through the right atrium, across a transseptal puncture into the left atrium, with a balloon inflated at the mitral valve. What procedure is being performed?

explanation.summary: A catheter reaches the left atrium via a transseptal puncture, and a balloon is inflated across the stenotic mitral orifice to split the fused commissures. This percutaneous balloon mitral valvuloplasty relieves obstruction in favorable rheumatic mitral stenosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: A catheter reaches the left atrium via a transseptal puncture, and a balloon is inflated across the stenotic mitral orifice to split the fused commissures. This percutaneous balloon mitral valvuloplasty relieves obstruction in favorable rheumatic mitral stenosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Annuloplasty rings are sewn surgically around the annulus, not delivered by a transseptal balloon catheter.
whyWrongByChoice.B: TAVR is usually delivered via the femoral artery retrogradely to the aortic valve, not transseptally to the mitral valve.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pulmonary vein ablation uses an energy catheter at the pulmonary vein ostia, not a balloon inflated across the mitral valve.

questions.topicName: Mitral Stenosis
questions.stem: This illustration traces a clot forming in the heart and lodging in a cerebral artery, with atrial fibrillation labeled at the heart. In a patient with mitral stenosis, what best explains this sequence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aortic atherosclerotic plaque ruptures and showers the cerebral arteries

choices.label: B
choices.text: Carotid stenosis alone produces the obstruction, unrelated to the heart

choices.label: C
choices.text: Right-to-left shunting sends venous clots directly into the carotid

choices.label: D
choices.text: Endocarditis vegetations embolize from the aortic valve

choices.label: E
choices.text: Left atrial stasis and atrial fibrillation promote thrombus that embolizes to the brain

explanation.summary: Mitral stenosis dilates the left atrium and predisposes to atrial fibrillation. Blood stasis in the fibrillating, enlarged atrium fosters thrombus formation; dislodged clot travels through the systemic circulation and can occlude a cerebral artery, producing a cardioembolic stroke.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mitral stenosis dilates the left atrium and predisposes to atrial fibrillation. Blood stasis in the fibrillating, enlarged atrium fosters thrombus formation; dislodged clot travels through the systemic circulation and can occlude a cerebral artery, producing a cardioembolic stroke.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aortic plaque can embolize, but the illustrated clot forms within the heart in the setting of atrial fibrillation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Carotid stenosis causes artery-to-artery emboli unrelated to the heart, whereas this clot originates in the heart.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Paradoxical embolism through a right-to-left shunt starts with venous thrombus; mitral stenosis instead creates clot within the left atrium.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Vegetations require infection and arise on valves; the sequence shows a clot from a fibrillating atrium.

questions.topicName: Mitral Stenosis
questions.stem: This gross specimen shows a mitral valve viewed from the atrium with a narrowed, slit-like central orifice and thickened, retracted leaflets. What diagnosis does this appearance represent?

choices.label: B
choices.text: A flail leaflet from ruptured chordae

choices.label: C
choices.text: A normal, widely patent mitral valve

choices.label: E
choices.text: Mitral stenosis with a fish-mouth orifice

explanation.summary: Chronic (usually rheumatic) inflammation fuses the commissures and thickens the leaflets, reducing the opening to a narrow fish-mouth slit. This is the classic gross appearance of mitral stenosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chronic (usually rheumatic) inflammation fuses the commissures and thickens the leaflets, reducing the opening to a narrow fish-mouth slit. This is the classic gross appearance of mitral stenosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A bicuspid valve is an aortic valve with two cusps, not a mitral valve viewed from the atrium.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A flail leaflet everts into the atrium from chordal rupture and causes regurgitation, not a narrowed slit-like orifice.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A normal mitral valve has thin, pliable leaflets and a wide orifice, unlike these thickened, retracted leaflets.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Vegetations are irregular friable masses on the leaflet surface, not diffuse thickening with a narrowed orifice.

questions.topicName: Mitral Stenosis
questions.stem: This gross specimen (panel C) shows a mitral valve with a reduced orifice and an arrow pointing to yellow-tan nodular material along the thickened leaflet. What does the arrowed material most likely represent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fresh red thrombus adherent to the leaflet

choices.label: C
choices.text: Myxomatous ground substance expanding the leaflet

choices.label: E
choices.text: Calcific deposits within the fibrotic stenotic valve

explanation.summary: Long-standing mitral stenosis leads to fibrosis with dystrophic calcification of the leaflets and commissures. The firm yellow-tan nodular deposits indicated by the arrow are calcium, which stiffens the valve and further narrows the orifice.
explanation.whyCorrect: Long-standing mitral stenosis leads to fibrosis with dystrophic calcification of the leaflets and commissures. The firm yellow-tan nodular deposits indicated by the arrow are calcium, which stiffens the valve and further narrows the orifice.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fresh thrombus is red and soft, while the arrowed material is firm, yellow-tan, and nodular.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fatty streaks occur in arterial intima, not on fibrotic mitral leaflets, and are flat rather than nodular.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Myxomatous change produces soft, gelatinous, redundant leaflets, not firm nodules on a stenotic valve.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Infective vegetations are friable, irregular, and destroy tissue, whereas these deposits are firm nodules within fibrotic leaflets.

questions.topicName: Mitral Stenosis
questions.stem: This diagram compares a normal heart with one showing mitral valve stenosis, where the mitral orifice is narrowed as blood passes from the left atrium to the left ventricle. What is the principal hemodynamic consequence of the narrowing shown?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Impaired diastolic filling of the left ventricle

choices.label: B
choices.text: Reduced afterload allowing rapid ventricular emptying

choices.label: C
choices.text: Backflow from the aorta into the left ventricle in diastole

choices.label: D
choices.text: Systolic backflow from the left ventricle into the left atrium

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increased forward stroke volume from the left ventricle

explanation.summary: A narrowed mitral orifice obstructs flow from the left atrium into the left ventricle during diastole. Pressure builds behind the valve, raising left atrial and pulmonary venous pressures while the left ventricle remains underfilled, producing the diastolic rumble and pulmonary congestion of mitral stenosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: A narrowed mitral orifice obstructs flow from the left atrium into the left ventricle during diastole. Pressure builds behind the valve, raising left atrial and pulmonary venous pressures while the left ventricle remains underfilled, producing the diastolic rumble and pulmonary congestion of mitral stenosis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Mitral stenosis does not reduce afterload; it underfills the ventricle, which limits rather than speeds output.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Backflow from the aorta into the ventricle in diastole is aortic regurgitation, not mitral narrowing.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Systolic backflow into the left atrium is mitral regurgitation, which requires an incompetent rather than narrowed valve.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Underfilling of the left ventricle reduces, not increases, forward stroke volume.

questions.topicName: Mitral Stenosis
questions.stem: The left panel shows pressure-volume loops (normal vs mitral stenosis) and the right panel shows pressure tracings where left atrial pressure exceeds left ventricular pressure during diastole. What does this persistent diastolic LA-to-LV pressure difference represent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A regurgitant v wave from mitral incompetence

choices.label: D
choices.text: The systolic gradient across a stenotic aortic valve

choices.label: E
choices.text: The pressure drop across an obstructed pulmonary valve

explanation.summary: A normal open mitral valve allows LA and LV diastolic pressures to equalize. In mitral stenosis the narrowed orifice sustains a pressure gradient, so LA pressure stays above LV pressure throughout diastole. The PV loop also shows the reduced LV filling and smaller stroke volume that result.
explanation.whyCorrect: A normal open mitral valve allows LA and LV diastolic pressures to equalize. In mitral stenosis the narrowed orifice sustains a pressure gradient, so LA pressure stays above LV pressure throughout diastole. The PV loop also shows the reduced LV filling and smaller stroke volume that result.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A regurgitant v wave is a systolic left atrial pressure spike from mitral incompetence, not a sustained diastolic gradient.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ventricular-arterial coupling refers to systolic ejection into the aorta, not a diastolic difference between atrium and ventricle.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A systolic gradient across the aortic valve compares LV with aortic pressure during ejection, not LA with LV in diastole.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pulmonary valve obstruction creates a systolic RV-to-pulmonary artery gradient on the right side of the heart.
